verdict.root_cause: At 12:39:46, roughly five minutes before the alert, platform-automation lowered the memory limit on frauddetection-service to 200m and, unlike the three preceding lower-then-revert cycles in the same window, never reverted it [tr_89bc77785074]. The service's Kafka consume log runs at steady, healthy throughput up to 12:39:41 and then stops dead, with nothing at all through the end of the window and no startup or consumer-rejoin lines to indicate a recovered process [tr_15c794e4c603]. The silence begins within seconds of the limit being applied, which is what happens when a running JVM-style consumer is killed for exceeding a newly constrained memory ceiling and cannot come back up under it. The mechanism now in play is memory exhaustion against a ceiling the process cannot fit inside — the container is being killed for using more than it is allowed — so the failing service is frauddetectionservice itself, and the blast radius is confined to it.
verdict.reasoning: Two independent, mutually corroborating signals carry this: a change record placing an unreverted 200m memory limit on the service seconds before its logs cease [tr_89bc77785074], and a log stream that shows normal, undegraded processing right up to 12:39:41 and then total silence with no restart evidence [tr_15c794e4c603]. The change specialist ruled out deploys, flags, dependency bumps and non-resource config edits — the only change surface touched in the window was the memory limit [tr_89bc77785074] — which removes bad_deploy and ordinary bad_config from contention. The prior three episodes of the same lowering were each reverted and did not coincide with an incident; the distinguishing feature of this one is persistence [tr_89bc77785074], which ties the constraint's continued presence, not the act of editing, to the outage. I classify this resource_exhaustion rather than bad_config because the value is not semantically wrong in the way a wrong port or credential is — the service is failing because it cannot fit in the memory it is now allowed, which is exhaustion; the edit is how it started. Both metric dispatches contributed nothing: the error-ratio query returned zero samples in incident and baseline windows alike, and the specialist noted the selector used the unhyphenated label form while the log stream resolves under the hyphenated name, so the emptiness is a selector/instrumentation artifact and cannot be read as either a health signal or a crash signal [tr_5aa7ff6cd322] [tr_f44a263a2767].
open_questions: No OOM-kill event, container restart count, memory working-set or memory-limit metric was ever retrieved — the kill mechanism is inferred from the timing of the limit change against log silence, not directly observed [tr_5aa7ff6cd322] [tr_f44a263a2767].

Why the alert fired at 12:45:45 when the service went silent at 12:39:41 — roughly six minutes earlier — is unexplained; the alerting rule's evaluation delay or the actual detection path was never examined [tr_15c794e4c603].

Whether metrics exist for this service under the hyphenated label 'frauddetection-service'; every metric query used the unhyphenated form and returned empty, so no saturation evidence was actually attempted against a resolving selector [tr_f44a263a2767].

What the platform-automation loop is and why it repeatedly applies and withdraws this same limit every few hours [tr_89bc77785074] — a plain revert may be re-applied by the same loop, so the durable fix may require disabling or correcting the automation rather than editing the limit once.
Whether any downstream consumer of fraud-detection results is degraded; triage scoped the incident to one service and no dependency or caller was dispatched on.

alternatives.root_cause: The 200m memory limit is itself simply the wrong value for this workload, making the misconfiguration the failure rather than any exhaustion mechanism.
alternatives.why_not: The remediation is identical, but the mechanism is not: what breaks requests here is the process being killed for exceeding a ceiling, not a value naming a wrong address, port or credential. A limit lowered until a process dies for exceeding it is exhaustion in progress; the edit is only its origin. Demoted on taxonomy, not on evidence.

alternatives.root_cause: frauddetectionservice never actually failed; the log cutoff at 12:39:41 is a retention or ingestion artifact and the alert fired on absent telemetry rather than a real fault.
alternatives.why_not: The log specialist explicitly checked and rejected a missing-pipeline explanation — the stream returns non-empty data under the hyphenated label, so ingestion works and the stop is a behavioural change [tr_15c794e4c603]. The coincidence of that stop with an unreverted memory-limit reduction seconds earlier [tr_89bc77785074] is too tight to attribute to retention. It stays on the list only because no restart or OOM metric was ever obtained to confirm the process actually died.

proposal.expected_effect: Restoring the pre-12:39:46 memory limit (the same value the three earlier lower-then-revert cycles restored) and recreating the container should bring the process back up under a ceiling it fits inside. Observable in Loki under the hyphenated selector {service="frauddetection-service"}: new lines appear within a couple of minutes of the recreate, starting with startup/initialization and consumer-group join messages, followed by 'Consumed record with orderId ... updated total count to: N' lines resuming at the pre-incident cadence of a few seconds apart. The counter will restart from a low number rather than continuing from 623, which is itself the signal that a fresh process instance is running. Note that the two metric probes for this service returned empty in both incident and baseline windows under the unhyphenated label, so Prometheus error-ratio, restart-count and memory series cannot be used to confirm this — logs are the only confirming surface available, and that is a weakness of this proposal, not a strength.
proposal.if_wrong: No log lines at all under {service="frauddetection-service"} within 5 minutes of the recreate, or startup lines appear and then silence returns within a minute or two. Either would mean the memory ceiling was not the thing keeping the process down — the kill mechanism was never directly observed (no OOM-kill event, no restart count, no memory working-set or limit metric was ever retrieved), so the whole causal step from 'limit lowered at 12:39:46' to 'process killed at 12:39:41+' is inferred from timing alone. A second falsifier on a longer horizon: logs resume and then stop again roughly 10 minutes later, which would mean the platform-automation loop re-applied the constraint and the durable fix is to disable or correct that loop, not to edit the limit once. Also unexplained and not addressed here: why the alert fired at 12:45:45 when the service went silent at 12:39:41; if that six-minute gap has a different cause, this revert may leave the alerting condition standing.
proposal.risk: If the process did not die of memory exhaustion, this recreate destroys a running-but-quiet process for nothing and discards its in-process state (cache, and any uncommitted Kafka consumer position — the consume counter resets, so a small number of records may be reprocessed or the group may rebalance). The prior configuration recorded in change history shows the memory limit as unset (None) before the lowering; reverting therefore removes the ceiling entirely, so if this service genuinely has a memory leak, the unbounded process can grow and put pressure on other containers on the same host — the very condition the automation loop may have been built to contain. This is a one-shot fix against an actor that has applied and withdrawn this same limit four times in the window; it does not stop the loop and will likely be undone by it.
proposal.blast_radius: One service: frauddetectionservice, the only service in this incident's blast radius. Its container is recreated, so anything holding a connection to it sees a reset during the recreate, and its Kafka consumer group rebalances on rejoin. Triage never dispatched on dependencies or callers, so no downstream consumer of fraud-detection results has been checked — whoever reads fraud verdicts has already been getting nothing since 12:39:41 and should see that resume, but the identity of those consumers is unverified in this brief. The reverted value is a resource limit, not a dependency address, so no traffic moves to other services.

triage_judgement.reasoning: A single critical alert on frauddetectionservice with no open incidents and no other signal to dismiss it; a critical label alone warrants a look. Nothing in the alert pattern points to a specific fault class yet.
